A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ViMoGen, ViMoGen-228K and MBench. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison across the reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original MBench evaluations, model ablations, human-preference analyses and HumanML3D experiments, including appendix results.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, hybrid-model experiments, human-alignment results and filtering statistics.

M1.justification: The flow-matching DiT, adaptive T2M/M2M branches and distilled ViMoGen-light remain. v2 specifies parameter sharing, binary gating, noise construction and translation masking, but these elaborate the existing procedure rather than establish a changed proposed method.

E1.justification: The reported ViMoGen-228K corpus composition, selected optical datasets, 450-prompt MBench suite and HumanML3D evaluation are retained. Added comparisons and analyses use existing data and tasks; no additional evaluation domain or test scenario is established.

E2.justification: Table 2 expands the MBench comparison from four external baselines to seven by adding FineMoGen, MotionDiffuse and MotionCraft. MotionDiffuse previously appeared only in the HumanML3D comparison. New Table 7 also evaluates MotionLCM/DNO model selection and hybrids replacing individual ViMoGen branches, substantially broadening the comparisons.

E3.justification: v2 introduces branch-replacement and external-model-selection controls in Table 7. It also revises stated camera restrictions: v1 requires static-camera clips, while v2 describes rejecting shaky cameras and generating stable camera movement. These are reported protocol changes; the PDFs do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Table 7 tests the unified model against separate-model selection and hybrid branches. Figure 6 extends human-alignment validation from six quality dimensions to all nine dimensions, adding pose quality and both semantic metrics. Figure 9 adds filtering-stage attrition analysis. Together these substantially extend scrutiny of the model, benchmark and dataset construction.

E5.justification: HumanML3D retains 20 repeated evaluations and 95% confidence intervals. Figure 6 already reports correlation coefficients in v1; v2 explicitly names Spearman correlation and extends the same reporting practice to additional dimensions. No new seed counts, uncertainty procedures or significance tests are reported.

E6.justification: Shared MBench and HumanML3D table entries remain unchanged, but v2 substantially expands the reported results. Additions include three baseline rows, hybrid comparisons such as MotionLCM+DNO scoring 0.49 consistency and 0.63 generalizability, human-alignment correlations of 0.8 for pose quality and 1.0 for each semantic dimension, and filtering-stage counts in Figure 9.

T1.justification: The flow-matching equations, motion representation and human-preference scoring rules are retained. The additional explanations introduce no new theoretical assumptions, propositions, proofs or substantive mathematical derivations.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction narrow the generalization-bottleneck claim explicitly to text-to-motion, excluding audio/music synthesis. The three principal contributions and the main performance claims remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds an interpretation of mutual benefits through shared branch parameters and explicit limitations concerning single-person generation and distorted high-dynamic video priors. It also explains weak human correlation for foot floating, ties induced by binary semantic scores, and the large volume of discarded video data. These substantially expand mechanism explanations and applicability qualifications.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents approximately 66% parameter sharing, Gaussian corruption ranges, jitter parameters, temporal dropout and translation masking, and adds a detailed preprocessing diagram. Existing hardware, optimizer, training budgets and branch probabilities are retained. Code and data release remains a future promise.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for FineMoGen, MotionCraft and DNO alongside their experimental comparisons. Appendix B and the broader positioning against conventional motion generation and video-derived motion methods remain essentially unchanged.

P1.justification: Focused rewrites clarify training versus inference and benchmark interpretation. v2 adds limitations, ethics, reproducibility and acknowledgement passages, updates author/header information, and promotes implementation details from Appendix D.3 to Appendix E. Most existing prose and the overall narrative structure are retained.

P2.justification: Several central displays change substantially: Figure 4 replaces seven pose-montage columns with four temporal-sequence columns, Figure 6 expands from six to nine panels, and v2 adds Table 7 plus preprocessing and filtering Figures 8–9. Table 2 gains comparator rows. Other appendix illustrations are retained with relocation and renumbering.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens comparison coverage, supplies the three previously unshown human-alignment dimensions, and makes noise simulation and failure limits more explicit. These improve evidential support and reproducibility. The gain is limited: Table 7 compares different component models, so its stronger interpretation about benefits from parameter sharing is not cleanly isolated.
